title: Christ Healing the Blind
credit: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Charles Wrightsman, 1978
caption_tea: Painted in Venice around 1570, before El Greco ever set foot in Spain, the work shows him absorbing Venetian Renaissance lessons in perspective and gesture; he left the upper-left corner unfinished, offering a rare glimpse of his loose underlying sketch.
caption_basic: Christ Healing the Blind by El Greco (ca. 1570) -- Oil on canvas

title: Cardinal Fernando Niño de Guevara
credit: H. O. Havemeyer Collection, Bequest of Mrs. H. O. Havemeyer, 1929
caption_tea: Niño de Guevara became Spain's inquisitor general in 1599, and El Greco likely painted him the following year on official Inquisition business in Toledo; painter Mary Cassatt spotted the portrait and urged the Havemeyers to buy it, a purchase that took collector Louisine Havemeyer four difficult years to pull off.
caption_basic: Cardinal Fernando Niño de Guevara by El Greco (ca. 1600) -- Oil on canvas

title: The Vision of Saint John
caption_tea: Painted in the last years of El Greco's life for a Toledo hospital church, this apocalyptic vision of martyred souls receiving robes of salvation was cut down from a larger altarpiece and later studied intently by Picasso while he was developing Les Demoiselles d'Avignon.
caption_basic: The Vision of Saint John by El Greco (ca. 1608–14) -- Oil on canvas

title: Ignacio Garcini y Queralt, Brigadier of Engineers
caption_tea: Goya painted this portrait of the military engineer Ignacio Garcini as a pendant to his wife Josefa's likeness in the same year, 1804; the pair stayed together in the Garcini family for over a century before entering the Met's collection through the same bequest.
caption_basic: Ignacio Garcini y Queralt, Brigadier of Engineers by Francisco de Goya (1804) -- Oil on canvas

title: Josefa de Castilla Portugal y van Asbrock de Garcini
caption_tea: Painted as a pendant to Goya's portrait of her husband, Colonel Ignacio Garcini, this informal portrait of Josefa -- loose-haired, in a simple dress, holding a small fan -- stayed in the Garcini family for over a century before both paintings were sold in 1910 and eventually bequeathed to the Met.
caption_basic: Josefa de Castilla Portugal y van Asbrock de Garcini by Francisco de Goya (1804) -- Oil on canvas

title: Wolf and Fox Hunt
caption_tea: This monumental canvas, painted with workshop assistants in 1616, was the first in a new genre Rubens essentially invented: giant hunting scenes that offered wealthy patrons a cheaper, faster alternative to tapestries -- though Rubens insisted the wolves themselves were painted entirely by his own hand.
caption_basic: Wolf and Fox Hunt by Peter Paul Rubens (ca. 1616) -- Oil on canvas

title: Self-Portrait
caption_tea: Van Dyck likely painted this self-portrait around age twenty-one, during a stay at the English court in the winter of 1620-21, not long before he left for Italy to spend six formative years studying Titian's color and brushwork.
caption_basic: Self-Portrait by Anthony van Dyck (ca. 1620–21) -- Oil on canvas

title: Madonna and Child
caption_tea: This is one of only two paintings that can be confidently attributed to Berlinghiero, the leading painter of Lucca in his day; it follows the Byzantine Hodegetria type -- "She Who Shows the Way" -- that reached Italy after icons flowed west following the fall of Constantinople in 1204.
caption_basic: Madonna and Child by Berlinghiero (possibly 1230s) -- Tempera on wood, gold ground

title: Madonna and Child
caption_tea: Bellini pulls back the curtain behind the Madonna to reveal a landscape shifting from barren hills to a lush, verdant town -- a quiet visual metaphor for resurrection and renewal behind the sacred scene.
caption_basic: Madonna and Child by Giovanni Bellini (late 1480s) -- Oil on wood

title: Virgin and Child with Saint Catherine of Alexandria
caption_tea: Saint Catherine, shown here with the pearls and martyr's palm of a princess, was venerated by young women for her legendary "mystical marriage" to Christ; the painting's warmth and rhythm reflect how deeply Van Dyck had absorbed Titian and Veronese during his years working in Italy.
caption_basic: Virgin and Child with Saint Catherine of Alexandria by Anthony van Dyck (ca. 1630) -- Oil on canvas

title: Virgin and Child with the Young Saint John the Baptist and Angels
credit: Gift of Adelaide Milton de Groot, 1966
caption_tea: Boucher painted this intimate devotional scene in 1765, the same year he was named director of the French Royal Academy, tucking Eucharistic grapes and the young Baptist's lamb into what could almost pass for a pastoral idyll.
caption_basic: Virgin and Child with the Young Saint John the Baptist and Angels by François Boucher (1765) -- Oil on canvas

title: The Collector of Prints
credit: H. O. Havemeyer Collection, Bequest of Mrs. H. O. Havemeyer, 1929
caption_tea: The identity of the print collector Degas painted has never been confirmed, but the room around him is filled with things Degas himself loved to collect -- Japanese fabric, Redouté-style botanical lithographs, and a Tang dynasty figurine -- turning the sitter's obsession into a mirror of the artist's own.
caption_basic: The Collector of Prints by Edgar Degas (1866) -- Oil on canvas

title: James-Jacques-Joseph Tissot (1836–1902)
caption_tea: Degas and Tissot were close friends from their student days in Florence, and here Degas surrounds him with signs of his artistic ambitions, including a copy of a Northern Renaissance portrait and a Japanese-style painting on the studio wall behind him.
caption_basic: James-Jacques-Joseph Tissot (1836–1902) by Edgar Degas (ca. 1867–68) -- Oil on canvas

title: The Little Fourteen-Year-Old Dancer
credit: H. O. Havemeyer Collection, Bequest of Mrs. H. O. Havemeyer, 1929
caption_tea: Degas modeled this on Marie van Goethem, a young Belgian student at the Paris Opera Ballet school, and it was the only sculpture he ever exhibited in his lifetime -- the original 1881 wax figure wore a real cotton bodice, linen ballet slippers, and a human-hair wig, and the Met has restrung and replaced this bronze cast's fabric tutu at least three times since acquiring it.
caption_basic: The Little Fourteen-Year-Old Dancer by Edgar Degas (1922 (cast)) -- Tinted bronze, cotton, silk, wood

title: At the Milliner's
medium: Pastel on pale gray wove paper (industrial wrapping paper), laid down on silk bolting
credit: H. O. Havemeyer Collection, Bequest of Mrs. H. O. Havemeyer, 1929
caption_tea: This pastel was the first of Degas's millinery-shop scenes to be shown publicly, at an 1882 exhibition in London; he became fascinated with the Paris hat trade, closely studying how feathers, flowers, and straw were arranged and sold to fashionable customers.
caption_basic: At the Milliner's by Edgar Degas (1882) -- Pastel on pale gray wove paper (industrial wrapping paper), laid down on silk bolting

title: L'Arlésienne: Madame Joseph-Michel Ginoux (Marie Julien, 1848–1911)
caption_tea: Marie Ginoux ran the Café de la Gare in Arles, where Van Gogh lodged in 1888. When Gauguin visited that November, the two artists painted her in the same sitting, with Gauguin sketching her in charcoal in under an hour while Van Gogh completed a full canvas.
caption_basic: L'Arlésienne: Madame Joseph-Michel Ginoux (Marie Julien, 1848–1911) by Vincent van Gogh (1888–89) -- Oil on canvas

title: Wheat Field with Cypresses
caption_tea: Painted directly outdoors during Van Gogh's stay at the asylum in Saint-Rémy, this canvas was one he later singled out as among his best summer landscapes, and he went on to make two further studio versions of the same composition. He also sent his brother Theo reed-pen drawings of the scene to describe its effect.
caption_basic: Wheat Field with Cypresses by Vincent van Gogh (1889) -- Oil on canvas

title: Irises
caption_tea: Van Gogh painted this bouquet in May 1890, just before checking himself out of the asylum at Saint-Rémy, pairing it with a canvas of roses in a deliberate exercise in complementary color contrast. He described his goal as a 'harmonious and soft' effect, though the violet blooms were originally set against a pink background that has since faded.
caption_basic: Irises by Vincent van Gogh (1890) -- Oil on canvas

title: The Triumph of Henry IV
caption_tea: This oil sketch was one small step toward a planned forty-eight-canvas cycle glorifying Marie de' Medici's husband, Henry IV, to hang alongside the queen's own completed cycle at the Palais du Luxembourg -- a companion series left mostly unfinished after Marie was banished from France in 1631.
caption_basic: The Triumph of Henry IV by Peter Paul Rubens (ca. 1630) -- Oil on wood

title: A Forest at Dawn with a Deer Hunt
credit: Purchase, The Annenberg Foundation and other gifts, 1990
caption_tea: Rubens painted this in the final years of his life after acquiring the manor of Het Steen in 1635, when hunting -- an aristocratic privilege -- suited his new identity as lord of his own estate; the scene's dawn light, filtered through Titian-inspired color and brushwork, casts the hunt as a contest between light and darkness itself.
caption_basic: A Forest at Dawn with a Deer Hunt by Peter Paul Rubens (ca. 1635) -- Oil on wood

title: Still Life with a Skull and a Writing Quill
caption_tea: Working in an almost monochrome palette of grays and browns, Claesz arranged a toppled glass, a gap-toothed skull, and a guttering oil lamp on a stone ledge that seems to extend into the viewer's own space, turning the still life into a blunt reminder of how quickly life passes.
caption_basic: Still Life with a Skull and a Writing Quill by Pieter Claesz (1628) -- Oil on wood

title: Still Life
caption_tea: Flegel is regarded as the first German painter to specialize in still life; over roughly thirty years in Frankfurt he produced around 110 small, tightly composed paintings of set tables, food, and flowers, of which this quiet arrangement is a rare survivor.
caption_basic: Still Life by Georg Flegel (probably ca. 1625–30) -- Oil on wood

title: The Silver Tureen
caption_tea: Chardin builds this still life around a quiet tension between the living and the dead: a cat crouches at the left eyeing a game rabbit and a dead bird laid out beside fruit and a gleaming silver tureen, each surface -- fur, feather, citrus peel, polished metal -- rendered convincingly without ever hiding the roughness of the paint itself.
caption_basic: The Silver Tureen by Jean Siméon Chardin (ca. 1728–30) -- Oil on canvas

title: Still Life: Balsam Apple and Vegetables
caption_tea: Peale arranged an unusually vivid array of vegetables, including okra, two kinds of cabbage, squash, eggplant, tomatoes, and the spiky orange balsam apple, in colors brighter than his usual subdued palette, making this one of his most celebrated still lifes.
caption_basic: Still Life: Balsam Apple and Vegetables by James Peale (ca. 1820s) -- Oil on canvas

title: Still Life with Teapot and Fruit
credit: The Walter H. and Leonore Annenberg Collection, Gift of Walter H. and Leonore Annenberg, 1997, Bequest of Walter H. Annenberg, 2002
caption_tea: Gauguin modeled this composition on a Cézanne still life he owned and treasured, swapping in mangoes for apples and a Tahitian printed cloth for French wallpaper; a year after finishing this picture, deep in debt, he was forced to sell that prized Cézanne.
caption_basic: Still Life with Teapot and Fruit by Paul Gauguin (1896) -- Oil on canvas

title: Scenes of Witchcraft: Morning
credit: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund
caption_basic: Scenes of Witchcraft: Morning by Salvator Rosa (c. 1645–1649) -- oil on canvas

title: Scenes of Witchcraft: Day
credit: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund
caption_basic: Scenes of Witchcraft: Day by Salvator Rosa (c. 1645–1649) -- oil on canvas

title: Scenes of Witchcraft: Evening
credit: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund
caption_basic: Scenes of Witchcraft: Evening by Salvator Rosa (c. 1645–49) -- oil on canvas

title: Scenes of Witchcraft: Night
credit: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund
caption_basic: Scenes of Witchcraft: Night by Salvator Rosa (c. 1645–1649) -- oil on canvas

title: Two Poplars in the Alpilles near Saint-Rémy
credit: Bequest of Leonard C. Hanna Jr.
caption_basic: Two Poplars in the Alpilles near Saint-Rémy by Vincent van Gogh (1889) -- oil on fabric

title: The Large Plane Trees (Road Menders at Saint-Rémy)
caption_basic: The Large Plane Trees (Road Menders at Saint-Rémy) by Vincent van Gogh (1889) -- oil on fabric

title: Adeline Ravoux
credit: Bequest of Leonard C. Hanna Jr.
caption_basic: Adeline Ravoux by Vincent van Gogh (1890) -- oil on fabric

title: Self-portrait
credit: Purchase, Harris Brisbane Dick Fund, by exchange, Anonymous Gift, and Virginia Marvin Stoughton Bequest, 2006
caption_tea: Copley painted this tiny watercolor-on-ivory self-portrait, just over an inch tall, in 1769 as a wedding gift for his new wife Susanna Clarke, alongside a nearly identical pastel version now held at Winterthur Museum in Delaware.
caption_basic: Self-portrait by John Singleton Copley (1769) -- Watercolor on ivory

title: Plum blossoms
medium: Album of twelve leaves; ink on paper
credit: Edward Elliott Family Collection, Gift of Douglas Dillon, 1986
caption_tea: Jin Nong, one of the so-called Eight Eccentrics of Yangzhou, took up plum-blossom painting only in his late sixties, reportedly completing this album during a six-week stay at a friend's home in 1757. His branches range from exuberant, blossom-laden sprays to single, spare twigs, each paired with his own poetic inscriptions.
caption_basic: Plum blossoms by Jin Nong (dated 1757) -- Album of twelve leaves; ink on paper

title: Old Trees, Level Distance
medium: Handscroll; ink and color on silk
credit: Gift of John M. Crawford Jr., in honor of Douglas Dillon, 1981
caption_tea: Guo Xi was the leading landscape painter of the Northern Song court, and this handscroll is thought to be a late work made for a retiring official, its bare autumn trees and deepening mist lending the scene a wistful, valedictory mood. The composition follows his signature 'level-distance' formula, pairing tall foreground trees with a wide, misty river valley.
caption_basic: Old Trees, Level Distance by Guo Xi (ca. 1080) -- Handscroll; ink and color on silk

title: Night-Shining White
caption_tea: This ink portrait shows a fiery cavalry horse owned by the Tang emperor Xuanzong, its flaring nostrils and dancing hooves capturing the spirited character prized in the imperial stables. More than a thousand years of collectors' seals and inscriptions crowd the mounting, tracing the scroll's passage through generations of connoisseurs.
caption_basic: Night-Shining White by Han Gan (ca. 750) -- Handscroll; ink on paper

title: Fragrant Snow at Broken Bridge
credit: Ex coll.: C. C. Wang Family, Purchase, Gift of J. Pierpont Morgan, by exchange, 1973
caption_tea: Wang Mian was a peasant-born scholar who abandoned the imperial examinations and instead earned his living selling ink paintings of plum blossoms, one of the 'Four Gentlemen' flowers prized for symbolizing resilience through winter's hardship. Broken Bridge, near West Lake in Hangzhou, was already famous as a plum-viewing spot when he painted this scene.
caption_basic: Fragrant Snow at Broken Bridge by Wang Mian (14th century) -- Hanging scroll; ink on silk

title: The Horse Fair
caption_tea: To study the horse trade firsthand, Bonheur spent a year and a half sketching at Paris's Boulevard de l'Hôpital horse market dressed in men's clothing, which let her move unbothered through a business dominated by men. Cornelius Vanderbilt purchased the finished canvas, over eight feet high and sixteen feet long, in 1887 and donated it to the Museum immediately.
caption_basic: The Horse Fair by Rosa Bonheur (1852–55) -- Oil on canvas

title: Quilt, Presentation pattern
caption_tea: Simon is thought to have sold pre-cut, basted appliqué quilt blocks as kits to Baltimore needlewomen between 1846 and 1854. This quilt is nearly identical to a dated 1849 example made as a wedding gift, and its own inscription patch was cut away and replaced with plain fabric before quilting, erasing the name of whomever it once honored.
caption_basic: Quilt, Presentation pattern by Mary Hergenroder Simon (ca. 1849) -- Cotton and silk velvet

title: The Thinker
caption_tea: Originally titled The Poet, this figure was conceived to sit above the lintel of Rodin's monumental bronze doorway The Gates of Hell, brooding over the damned souls of Dante's Inferno below him; that vast doorway, commissioned for a museum that was never built, was never even cast in bronze during Rodin's own lifetime.
caption_basic: The Thinker by Auguste Rodin (modeled ca. 1880, cast ca. 1910) -- Bronze

title: Saint Bridget of Sweden Receiving the Rule of Her Order
caption_tea: This relief depicts a mystic vision that Saint Bridget recorded in her own writings, the Revelationes, in which Christ himself presents her with the rule for the religious order she founded in Sweden in 1346. Carved for an altar predella in Perugia that was dismantled just decades later, it portrays a subject rarely attempted in fifteenth-century sculpture.
caption_basic: Saint Bridget of Sweden Receiving the Rule of Her Order by Agostino d'Antonio di Duccio (1459) -- Marble

title: Watch
medium: Agate, onyx cameo, enameled gold, gemstones
caption_tea: The man carved into this watch's onyx cameo was long thought to be a sixteenth-century Fugger banker, but surviving Fugger portraits don't match him -- he more likely belongs to the early seventeenth-century "Dürer revival" fashion among Augsburg's goldsmiths and watchmakers.
caption_basic: Watch by Wilhelm Peffenhauser (ca. 1650) -- Agate, onyx cameo, enameled gold, gemstones

title: Bowl with cover (perfume burner)
caption_tea: Giuseppe de' Levi, a bronze founder probably of Jewish origin working in Verona, habitually signed his pieces -- this bowl carries a cast inscription on its underside reading, in translation, '1599, de Rossi and Giuseppe de Levi of Verona made this' -- and its decoration, though it likely held burning perfume, is entirely secular, made for a wealthy household's cabinet rather than any devotional use.
caption_basic: Bowl with cover (perfume burner) by Giuseppe de' Levi (1599) -- Bronze

title: Two-handled bowl from Burghley House, Lincolnshire
date: Chinese porcelain 1573– ca. 1585, British mounts ca. 1585
caption_tea: This Wanli-period blue-and-white bowl was fitted with English silver mounts almost as soon as it reached London, likely for Elizabeth I's chief minister William Cecil, Lord Burghley. The gilt-silver mounts borrow ornament from Antwerp design books, and the bowl later passed through the collections of J. Pierpont Morgan before reaching the Met.
caption_basic: Two-handled bowl from Burghley House, Lincolnshire (Chinese porcelain 1573– ca. 1585, British mounts ca. 1585) -- Hard-paste porcelain, gilded silver

title: Sabine Houdon (1787–1836)
medium: White marble on gray marble socle
caption_tea: This is a portrait of the sculptor's own daughter, one of a series of busts Houdon made of his three daughters as they grew; when it was sold at the 1928 auction of Judge Elbert H. Gary's collection it fetched $245,000, the highest price then ever paid for a sculpture at auction, a record it held for more than four decades.
caption_basic: Sabine Houdon (1787–1836) by Jean Antoine Houdon (1788) -- White marble on gray marble socle

title: Potpourri jar
medium: Soft-paste porcelain decorated in underglaze blue
credit: Gift of R. Thornton Wilson, in memory of Florence Ellsworth Wilson, 1950
caption_tea: This jar is one of only a handful of surviving pieces of Rouen soft-paste porcelain, a short-lived 1690s experiment to imitate Chinese porcelain that never reached commercial production. No museum outside France owns another example, making the Met's jar the only one abroad.
caption_basic: Potpourri jar by Louis Poterat Manufactory (ca. 1690–95) -- Soft-paste porcelain decorated in underglaze blue

title: Street vendor
credit: Gift of R. Thornton Wilson, in memory of Florence Ellsworth Wilson, 1954
caption_tea: Carved fully in the round, this porcelain figure only gives up its subject from certain angles: walk around it and the basket on the man's back turns out to be full of mushrooms he is peddling door to door, a popular type produced by the Mennecy factory under the protection of the Duc de Villeroy.
caption_basic: Street vendor by Mennecy (ca. 1750–60) -- Soft-paste porcelain

title: Pair of Wheellock Pistols
caption_tea: This dazzling pair of pistols was carved from steel, brass, gold, and ivory in Maastricht around 1655–65 — genuinely rare not for its opulence but its mechanism. Nearly every ivory-stocked Dutch pistol of the era was fitted with a flintlock; this wheellock pair is among the earliest surviving examples of its kind. A gift to the Met from collector William H. Riggs in 1913.
caption_basic: Pair of Wheellock Pistols (ca. 1655–65) -- Steel, brass, gold, ivory

tea_voice_sources.text: Nearly every ivory-stocked Dutch pistol of the era was fitted with a flintlock; this wheellock pair is among the earliest surviving examples of its kind.

title: Armor (Gusoku)
bio: Japanese, Edo period, active early–mid-19th century
culture: Japanese, Edo period, active early–mid-19th century
caption_tea: This gusoku is a composite spanning two centuries and two celebrated workshops. Its helmet bowl, signed by the armorer Saotome Ietada and marked with the Saotome family's telltale extra rivet — an unofficial second signature — dates to the 16th century, while the rest of the armor was assembled generations later for the armory of Date Yoshimura, daimyo of Sendai. The breastplate is inscribed with the name of its own maker, Myōchin Munesuke, whose embossed ironwork is the hallmark of the rival Myōchin school.
caption_basic: Armor (Gusoku) by Saotome Ietada (16th and 18th centuries) -- Iron, lacquer, silk, gilt copper

tea_voice_sources.text: This gusoku is a composite spanning two centuries and two celebrated workshops... assembled generations later for the armory of Date Yoshimura, daimyo of Sendai. The breastplate is inscribed with the name of its own maker, Myōchin Munesuke.
the Saotome family's telltale extra rivet — an unofficial second signature

title: Hunting Sword with Scabbard
credit: Gift of Jean Jacques Reubell, in memory of his mother, Julia C. Coster, and of his wife, Adeline E. Post, both of New York City, 1926
caption_tea: The ivory grip of this hunting sword, attributed to Joseph Deutschmann of Passau, is carved in full Rococo exuberance — shells, waves, and a lion gripping a crescent moon beneath its paw, probably alluding to Europe's recent victories over the Ottoman Turks. Made around 1740, it belongs to a tradition in which hunting swords were as much emblems of aristocratic rank as they were weapons, often commissioned in gold, silver, and ivory to match their owner's standing as much as their quarry.
caption_basic: Hunting Sword with Scabbard by Joseph Deutschmann (ca. 1740) -- Steel, silver, ivory, wood, leather

tea_voice_sources.text: carved in full Rococo exuberance — shells, waves, and a lion gripping a crescent moon beneath its paw, probably alluding to Europe's recent victories over the Ottoman Turks
hunting swords were as much emblems of aristocratic rank as they were weapons, often commissioned in gold, silver, and ivory to match their owner's standing

title: Helmet
caption_tea: Excavated from the Ōtsuka-yama burial mound in Mie Prefecture sometime before 1902, this iron, copper, and gold helmet dates to Japan's 5th-century Kofun period, when elite warriors were interred in earthen tumuli together with their weapons and armor. It passed through the collection of Dr. Seki Yasunosuke before being sold at auction in Kyoto in November 1927, reaching the Met via the Fletcher Fund the following year.
caption_basic: Helmet (5th century) -- Iron, copper, gold

tea_voice_sources.text: Excavated from the Ōtsuka-yama burial mound in Mie Prefecture sometime before 1902... passed through the collection of Dr. Seki Yasunosuke before being sold at auction in Kyoto in November 1927, reaching the Met via the Fletcher Fund the following year.
Japan's 5th-century Kofun period, when elite warriors were interred in earthen tumuli together with their weapons and armor

title: Shield (Pavise)
credit: Bashford Dean Memorial Collection, Funds from various donors, 1929
caption_tea: Painted with the coat of arms of Enns, a city in Upper Austria, this pavise belonged to a class of large standing shields carried by crossbowmen and other foot soldiers across 15th-century Central Europe. Fitted with a prop so it could stand upright on its own, it let an archer shelter behind it while reloading — a slow process that left crossbowmen exposed without one.
caption_basic: Shield (Pavise) (1450–1500) -- Wood, leather, gesso, polychromy

tea_voice_sources.text: Painted with the coat of arms of Enns, a city in Upper Austria
carried by crossbowmen and other foot soldiers... fitted with a prop so it could stand upright... let an archer shelter behind it while reloading

title: Sword
credit: The Collection of Giovanni P. Morosini, presented by his daughter Giulia, 1932
caption_tea: Carved into the pommel of this sword is a Latin motto — "Here virtue will find its reward" — a fitting inscription for a piece that outlived its own century by five hundred years. Made in Western Europe around 1400, it later passed through the collection of Giovanni P. Morosini before his daughter Giulia gave it to the Met in 1932.
caption_basic: Sword (ca. 1400) -- Steel, silver, copper alloy, leather

tea_voice_sources.text: Latin quote on the hilt's head reading: "Here virtue will find its reward"

title: Shield of Henry II of France (reigned 1547–59)
caption_tea: This parade shield, made for the French king Henry II around 1555, is thought to follow a design by Étienne Delaune — one of the most sought-after goldsmiths and engravers in Henry's own court armory, called on for the crown's most prestigious commissions.
caption_basic: Shield of Henry II of France (reigned 1547–59) (ca. 1555) -- Steel, gold, silver

tea_voice_sources.text: thought to have been based on a design by Étienne Delaune, one of the most skilled artisans in Henry's court armoury, called upon for the most prestigious commissions

title: Dagger
date: grip and blade, 16th century; guard, hallmarked for 1774–89
caption_tea: This dagger is itself a two-century collaboration: its ivory grip and blade were carved in the 16th century, while its guard was added nearly two hundred years later, hallmarked to the reign of Ottoman Sultan Abdulhamid I. The blade carries an inscribed couplet in Turkish and Persian, the languages of the Ottoman court: "I besought a drink of water from your trenchant dagger, what if but once you should let me drink, what would you lose?"
caption_basic: Dagger (grip and blade, 16th century; guard, hallmarked for 1774–89) -- Steel, ivory, gold, silver

tea_voice_sources.text: assembled during the reign of Sultan Abdulhamid I (r. 1774–89), incorporating a 16th-century grip and blade and an 18th-century guard; blade inscribed with a Turkish/Persian couplet

title: Helmet
caption_tea: Made in Germany around 1535, this fluted helmet belongs to a style that was already on its way out of fashion — one of the last, and among the largest, examples of its kind. Its banded scales and roped edging are hallmarks of armor associated with northern Germany, possibly the city of Brunswick.
caption_basic: Helmet (ca. 1535) -- Steel

tea_voice_sources.text: fine late example of fluted armor, made shortly before the style went out of fashion, unusually large proportions, features frequently found on armors from northern Germany (possibly Brunswick)

title: Armor of Henry II, King of France (reigned 1547–59)
caption_tea: One of the most elaborate French parade armors to survive intact, this suit was made around 1555 for Henry II of France from designs largely credited to Jean Cousin the Elder, with additional drawings by Étienne Delaune and Baptiste Pellerin — three of the most distinguished artists working in Paris at the time. Its surfaces are densely worked with mythological scenes: Apollo chasing the nymph Daphne on one shoulder, Apollo triumphant over the slain Python on the other, and the king's own crescent-moon badge worked in throughout.
caption_basic: Armor of Henry II, King of France (reigned 1547–59) by Jean Cousin the Elder (ca. 1555) -- Steel, gold, silver, leather, textile

tea_voice_sources.text: Twenty original design drawings survive: one by Jean Cousin the Elder, the rest by Étienne Delaune or Baptiste Pellerin; decoration includes Apollo chasing Daphne and Apollo with the slain Python; the crescent moon, a badge of Henry II, appears throughout

title: Esneh (Latopolis), Construction Ensablée - Architrave, Futs, et Chapiteaux
medium: Salted paper print from paper negative
caption_tea: Teynard was a civil engineer, not a professional photographer, who traveled more than a thousand miles up the Nile in 1851-52 to update Napoleon's decades-old "Description de l'Égypte" survey. His 160 salted-paper prints formed the most complete photographic record of the Nile Valley made to that date, though fewer than a dozen complete sets of the finished portfolio survive today.
caption_basic: Esneh (Latopolis), Construction Ensablée - Architrave, Futs, et Chapiteaux by Félix Teynard (1851–52, printed 1853–54) -- Salted paper print from paper negative

title: [The Great Wave, Sète]
medium: Albumen silver print from glass negative
caption_tea: 1850s photographic plates could not register both sea and sky in one exposure without one washing out, so Le Gray printed two different negatives, one for the water and one for the clouds, onto the same sheet of paper. The seam is faintly visible at the horizon, but the trick made this one of the first photographs to convincingly freeze a moving sea.
caption_basic: [The Great Wave, Sète] by Gustave Le Gray (1857) -- Albumen silver print from glass negative

title: Black Cañon, From Camp 8, Looking Above
medium: Albumen silver print from glass negative
credit: Purchase, Joseph Pulitzer Bequest and The Horace W. Goldsmith Foundation Gift through Joyce and Robert Menschel, 1986
caption_tea: O'Sullivan, a veteran Civil War photographer, joined Lieutenant George Wheeler's 1871 survey of the Colorado River and was given his own boat to haul his glass-plate darkroom through the rapids. His images of Black Canyon are among the earliest photographs of a landscape later submerged by the reservoirs of the Hoover and Davis dams.
caption_basic: Black Cañon, From Camp 8, Looking Above by Timothy H. O'Sullivan (1871) -- Albumen silver print from glass negative

title: Caroline Nightingale
medium: Albumen silver print from glass negative
caption_tea: Most surviving Victorian albumen portraits of private sitters like this one came from small, anonymous local studios rather than famous names, since the vast majority of 1870s portrait photographers never signed their prints. Here the sitter's identity, preserved only by an inscription, has outlasted any record of who actually made the picture.
caption_basic: Caroline Nightingale (1875) -- Albumen silver print from glass negative

title: [The Harvey Album]
credit: Purchase, The Horace W. Goldsmith Foundation Gift, through Joyce and Robert Menschel, 1998
caption_tea: Emily Clare Harvey made this album as a wedding gift for her sister-in-law in 1868, hand-painting watercolor borders around each pasted-in photograph, hunting motifs around a brother's portrait, flowers symbolizing affection around a female relative's, turning mass-produced studio cartes de visite into a one-of-a-kind keepsake.
caption_basic: [The Harvey Album] by Emily Clare Harvey (1868) -- Albumen silver print

title: Bourges
medium: Salted paper print from paper negative
credit: Gilman Collection, Purchase, The Horace W. Goldsmith Foundation Gift, through Joyce and Robert Menschel, 2005
caption_tea: For more than a century, the photographer who signed his salted-paper prints "Em. Pec" was unidentified in any photographic society record. Only in 2002 did research finally confirm him as Pierre-Émile-Joseph Pécarrère, a lawyer who had learned photography from Gustave Le Gray and photographed Gothic architecture across France in the early 1850s.
caption_basic: Bourges by Pierre Emile Joseph Pécarrère (1850–52) -- Salted paper print from paper negative

title: Emancipated Slaves Brought from Louisiana by Colonel George H. Hanks
medium: Albumen silver print from glass negative
credit: Gilman Collection, Purchase, The Horace W. Goldsmith Foundation Gift, through Joyce and Robert Menschel, 2005
caption_tea: In December 1863 a Union colonel brought eight formerly enslaved children and adults from occupied New Orleans to be photographed in New York, and cartes de visite like this one were sold to raise money for freedpeople's schools. One version of the image, captioned "White and Black Slaves from New Orleans," was designed to unsettle viewers who assumed slavery was visibly marked by skin color.
caption_basic: Emancipated Slaves Brought from Louisiana by Colonel George H. Hanks by Myron H. Kimball (December 1863) -- Albumen silver print from glass negative

title: [Mugshots of Suspected Anarchists from French Police Files]
medium: Albumen silver prints and gelatin silver prints
caption_tea: Alphonse Bertillon, a Paris police clerk, invented the modern mug shot, a standardized front-and-profile photograph paired with precise body measurements, and applied it on a mass scale to anarchist suspects rounded up after a wave of bombings in the early 1890s. His method, called Bertillonage, was adopted by police departments worldwide before fingerprinting eventually replaced it.
caption_basic: [Mugshots of Suspected Anarchists from French Police Files] by Alphonse Bertillon (1891–95) -- Albumen silver prints and gelatin silver prints

title: Egypt, from the Du Camp album
caption_tea: Working with a bulky wooden calotype camera and glass jugs of chemicals lugged across the desert, Du Camp produced negatives that were printed onto salted paper by the Lille firm of Blanquart-Évrard for his landmark 1852 album -- one of photography's first great travel books.
caption_basic: Egypt, from the Du Camp album by Maxime Du Camp (1849–51) -- Salted paper print

title: Egypt, from the Du Camp album
caption_tea: Maxime Du Camp made these views while traveling up the Nile with his friend, the future novelist Gustave Flaubert, hauling a wooden calotype camera, a tripod, and jugs of chemicals across Egypt between 1849 and 1851; the resulting album, published in 1852, is considered the first French book ever illustrated with photographs.
caption_basic: Egypt, from the Du Camp album by Maxime Du Camp (1849–51) -- Salted paper print

title: Self-Portrait
medium: Brush and point of brush, carbon black ink
caption_tea: Goya made this brush-and-ink self-portrait not long after a severe illness in 1792–93 left him permanently deaf; the drawing's searching, inward gaze is often read as a record of the isolated interior world he inhabited after losing his hearing.
caption_basic: Self-Portrait by Goya (Francisco de Goya y Lucientes) (ca. 1796) -- Brush and point of brush, carbon black ink

title: Mascarade à la Grecque; Suite des Vases
caption_tea: Petitot invented these fantastical costumes -- a shepherdess, a priestess, a monk, a sutler in outlandish architectural dress -- as a gentle joke aimed at the "Greek taste" craze that swept French fashion and design in the 1750s.
caption_basic: Mascarade à la Grecque; Suite des Vases by Ennemond Alexandre Petitot (1764–71) -- Etching

title: An Apostle
credit: Harris Brisbane Dick Fund, by exchange, 1970
caption_tea: Almost nothing is recorded about Angiolo Falconetto beyond a small handful of surviving etchings, including companion prints of Saint James Major and Saint Matthew -- suggesting this apostle was originally one figure in a now-scattered series, a rare trace of a printmaker who otherwise left barely a mark on history.
caption_basic: An Apostle by Angiolo Falconetto (ca. 1555–67) -- Etching

title: Print after Orazio Samacchini
caption_tea: This anonymous etching mirrors, in reverse, a painting by the Bolognese Mannerist Orazio Samacchini now in the Pinacoteca Nazionale in Bologna -- a reminder that reproductive prints like this one were how most people in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries ever got to "see" a famous altarpiece they could never visit in person.
caption_basic: Print after Orazio Samacchini by Anonymous (ca. 1570–1650) -- Etching

title: A Sibyl Reading a Book Facing Left
artist: After Raphael; print attributed to Ugo da Carpi
caption_tea: Ugo da Carpi is credited as the first Italian printmaker to master the chiaroscuro woodcut -- building an image from several wood blocks inked in different tones to mimic a wash drawing -- and he was proud enough of the invention to win an exclusive printing privilege from the Venetian Senate in 1516, followed by a papal privilege in 1518, the year this sheet after Raphael's design was made.
caption_basic: A Sibyl Reading a Book Facing Left by After Raphael; print attributed to Ugo da Carpi (ca. 1518) -- Chiaroscuro woodcut

title: Self-Portrait
medium: Watercolor, graphite, and gouache on paper
caption_tea: This watercolor is one of dozens of unflinching self-portraits Schiele made between 1910 and 1918, and it once belonged to Scofield Thayer, an American poet and Freud patient in Vienna who assembled a major collection of Schiele's and Klimt's work while undergoing psychoanalysis in the early 1920s.
caption_basic: Self-Portrait by Egon Schiele (1911) -- Watercolor, graphite, and gouache on paper

title: Six Jewel Rivers from Various Provinces
medium: Six woodblock prints; ink and color on paper
credit: Mary Griggs Burke Collection, Gift of the Mary and Jackson Burke Foundation, 2015
caption_tea: Each print in this series pairs a classical poem with a scene of women at one of Japan's celebrated 'Tama' rivers, washing or pounding cloth by moonlight, turning an old courtly poetic theme into everyday genre scenes of women's work.
caption_basic: Six Jewel Rivers from Various Provinces by Utagawa Hiroshige (1857) -- Six woodblock prints; ink and color on paper

title: The Art of Conversation
medium: Woodblock print; ink and color on paper
credit: Gift of Estate of Samuel Isham, 1914
caption_tea: Suzuki Harunobu was the innovator behind nishiki-e, the full-color woodblock printing technique he helped pioneer around 1765, using multiple hand-carved blocks to layer color onto paper in a process that transformed Japanese printmaking almost overnight.
caption_basic: The Art of Conversation by Suzuki Harunobu (Edo period) -- Woodblock print; ink and color on paper

title: Encyclopedia of Western Art (Kōmō Zatsuwa)
caption_tea: Published during Japan's era of Rangaku, or "Dutch Learning," this five-volume illustrated book gathered Morishima Chūryō's notes on European geography, customs, and curiosities gleaned from conversations with the Dutch traders confined to the man-made island of Dejima -- Japan's only officially sanctioned window onto the West during its centuries of seclusion.
caption_basic: Encyclopedia of Western Art (Kōmō Zatsuwa) by Morishima Chūryō (1787) -- Ink on paper

title: Landscape with Bridge
credit: Museum purchase through gift of various donors
caption_tea: Felice Giani was one of the leading Neoclassical decorators of his age, best known for elaborate wall and ceiling schemes in palaces and villas across Italy and France, including the Palazzo Milzetti in Faenza and Rome's Palazzo Quirinale — drawing frequently on subjects from Greek and Roman history and literature. The Cooper Hewitt holds one of the largest collections of his works on paper outside Italy, hundreds of drawings strong.
caption_basic: Landscape with Bridge by Felice Giani (late 18th–early 19th century) -- Pen and ink on paper

tea_voice_sources.text: Giani prolific painter and draftsman, best known for decorative wall/ceiling schemes including Palazzo Milzetti and Palazzo Quirinale, Neoclassical style drawing on Greek/Roman subjects; Cooper Hewitt holds one of the largest collections of his works on paper outside Italy

title: Bell Tower
caption_tea: Robert Frederick Blum made this drawing around the time he first arrived in Venice in 1880, at the start of a two-year stay that put him in the orbit of an international circle of expatriate artists. He lived as a neighbor to James McNeill Whistler, who introduced him to the principles of Japanese design and encouraged him to take up pastels — influences that would shape his work for years after he left the city.
caption_basic: Bell Tower by Robert Frederick Blum (1880) -- Graphite on wove paper

tea_voice_sources.text: Blum first visited Venice in 1880, joining William Merritt Chase; neighbor to James McNeill Whistler, who instructed him in Japanese design principles and encouraged his use of pastels

title: Front elevation of the house of Mr. Gédéon Mallet in Geneva
medium: Pencil, pen and ink, watercolor on paper
credit: Purchased for the Museum by the Advisory Council
caption_tea: This is Jean-François Blondel's own elevation for the house of Monsieur Gédéon Mallet in Geneva, built around 1724 — one of the architect's documented residential commissions, detailed enough that a companion drawing survives showing the side elevations of the house's right wing as well.
caption_basic: Front elevation of the house of Mr. Gédéon Mallet in Geneva by Jean François Blondel (ca. 1725) -- Pencil, pen and ink, watercolor on paper

tea_voice_sources.text: Maison Mallet in Geneva constructed 1724, a notable work of Jean-François Blondel; a companion drawing of the side elevations of the house's right wing survives in the same collection

title: Elevation of a Mausoleum for a Soldier (Temple of Mars)
medium: Pen and black ink, brush and black, gray wash over black chalk indications on off-white laid paper, lined
credit: Purchased for the Museum by the Advisory Council
caption_tea: Jean-Charles Delafosse produced a series of seventeen ruin-fantasy and mausoleum designs between 1765 and 1775, of which this elevation is one — drawings that bridged artistic imagination and academic architectural theory, positioning his work as scholarly invention rather than mere ornament.
caption_basic: Elevation of a Mausoleum for a Soldier (Temple of Mars) by Jean-Charles Delafosse (ca. 1765) -- Pen and black ink, brush and black, gray wash over black chalk indications on off-white laid paper, lined

tea_voice_sources.text: Delafosse produced 17 significant architectural and ruin-fantasy drawings between 1765-1775, reflecting academic and decorative ambitions, bridging artistic imagination and mechanical building practice

title: Study of Siena Cathedral
caption_tea: Walter Shirlaw made this study not long after a formative stretch abroad: barred from settling in Paris by the outbreak of the Franco-Prussian War, he studied instead in Munich, where he fell in with a circle of American painters that included Frank Duveneck and William Merritt Chase. He would go on to become the first president of the Society of American Artists and teach for years at New York's Art Students League.
caption_basic: Study of Siena Cathedral by Walter Shirlaw (ca. 1872) -- Graphite and watercolor on paper

tea_voice_sources.text: in 1870 Shirlaw traveled to Europe to study; prevented from settling in Paris by the Franco-Prussian War, studied in Munich with Frank Duveneck and William Merritt Chase; founder and first president of the Society of American Artists, teacher at the Art Students League

title: Hohensalzburg Fortress, Salzburg, Austria
medium: Oil and graphite on bright green paperboard
caption_tea: Frederic Edwin Church made this study of the Hohensalzburg Fortress during a trip through Austria in the summer of 1868, working directly in oil on paperboard rather than canvas — a quick, on-the-spot method he used often on his travels to capture a place before painting a finished work later, back in the studio.
caption_basic: Hohensalzburg Fortress, Salzburg, Austria by Frederic Edwin Church (June - July 1868) -- Oil and graphite on bright green paperboard

tea_voice_sources.text: Church painted the Hohensalzburg Fortress, Salzburg, dated 1868-69, oil sketch on paperboard

title: Circular Pedestal in the Dionysus Theater, Athens, Greece
medium: Brush and oil paint, graphite on tan paperboard
caption_tea: Church spent several weeks in Athens in the spring of 1869, filling sketchbooks with studies of the Acropolis and its surrounding ruins that later served as the basis for finished paintings back in his studio — this sketch of a theater pedestal is one of the many architectural fragments he recorded on that trip.
caption_basic: Circular Pedestal in the Dionysus Theater, Athens, Greece by Frederic Edwin Church (April 1869) -- Brush and oil paint, graphite on tan paperboard

tea_voice_sources.text: Church visited Greece in 1869, spent several weeks in Athens making numerous sketches and oil studies of the ruins of the Acropolis that later served as the basis for finished paintings

title: Cathedral at Popayán, Colombia
caption_tea: Church made this graphite drawing in August 1853, partway through a months-long journey across Colombia and Ecuador undertaken in the spirit of Alexander von Humboldt's own accounts of the region. The trip and its resulting body of work are documented in Elaine Evans Dee's study of Church's drawings, "To Embrace the Universe."
caption_basic: Cathedral at Popayán, Colombia by Frederic Edwin Church (August 5, 1853) -- Graphite on white wove paper

tea_voice_sources.text: Church traveled through Colombia and Ecuador April-October 1853, inspired by Alexander von Humboldt's account of the region; drawing documented in Elaine Evans Dee's "To Embrace the Universe: Drawings by Frederic Edwin Church"

title: Garden Pavilion and Latticed Gallery with an Alternative Design plate 365 from the publication "L'Art de Treillageur ou menuiserie des jardins"
credit: Gift of Eleanor and Sarah Hewitt
caption_tea: This plate comes from André-Jacob Roubo's treatise on treillage — ornamental garden trelliswork carpentry — published in four volumes between 1769 and 1775, with this design appearing in the final volume devoted entirely to garden structures. Treillage of the kind Roubo systematized here was used extensively throughout the gardens of Versailles.
caption_basic: Garden Pavilion and Latticed Gallery with an Alternative Design plate 365 from the publication "L'Art de Treillageur ou menuiserie des jardins" by André-Jacob Roubo (1775) -- Engraving on off-white laid paper

tea_voice_sources.text: Roubo theorized treillage in L'art du treillageur ou menuiserie des jardins, published 1769-1775 in four volumes, final volume covering garden trellis work; treillage used extensively in the Gardens of Versailles

title: Elevation of the Facade of a Theater, Amsterdam
medium: Pen and gray washes on cream-colored paper
caption_basic: Elevation of the Facade of a Theater, Amsterdam by Cesare Recanatini (ca. 1860) -- Pen and gray washes on cream-colored paper

title: The Farnese Table
caption_tea: Designed for Cardinal Alessandro Farnese and weighing some thirty thousand pounds, this pietre-dure tabletop was so prized that whenever the cardinal traveled, servants covered it in leather and locked it inside a padlocked wooden case.
caption_basic: The Farnese Table by Jacopo Barozzi da Vignola (ca. 1565–73) -- Marble, semiprecious stones, Egyptian alabaster

title: Creamer with cover (part of a service)
credit: Helena Woolworth McCann Collection, Purchase, Winfield Foundation Gift, 1961
caption_tea: The Dutch East India Company commissioned the artist Cornelis Pronk to draw designs of women, birds, and landscapes that were shipped to China so Jingdezhen painters could copy them onto porcelain. Only a handful of complete Pronk-pattern services survive today, making pieces like this creamer rare.
caption_basic: Creamer with cover (part of a service) by Cornelis Pronk (ca. 1740) -- Hard-paste porcelain

title: Two Elevations of the Central Part of a Palace
medium: Pen and brown ink, brush and brown wash on off-white laid paper, lined
credit: Museum purchase through gift of various donors and from Eleanor G. Hewitt Fund
caption_tea: Giuseppe Barberi has been called one of the most inventive architects working in late 18th-century Italy, though his legacy survives mostly on paper rather than in built form — a torrent of ideal architectural projects, capricci, and theatrical set designs. This elevation, showing three wings facing a colonnaded courtyard, is part of that larger body of drawn, rarely realized architectural imagination.
caption_basic: Two Elevations of the Central Part of a Palace by Giuseppe Barberi (1792) -- Pen and brown ink, brush and brown wash on off-white laid paper, lined

tea_voice_sources.text: Barberi "one of the most fertile architects of the Italian late eighteenth century," noted for inventiveness with ideal architectural projects, capricci, theatrical set studies; related palace elevation drawing shows three wings facing a courtyard with colonnades

title: Elevation of a Palace
medium: Pen and brown ink, brush and brown wash on off-white laid paper, lined
credit: Museum purchase through gift of various donors and from Eleanor G. Hewitt Fund
caption_tea: Giuseppe Barberi's reputation rests almost entirely on paper: he's remembered as one of the most inventive architects of late 18th-century Italy, producing a torrent of ideal projects, capricci, and theatrical designs, most of which — like this palace elevation — were never built.
caption_basic: Elevation of a Palace by Giuseppe Barberi (1746–1809) -- Pen and brown ink, brush and brown wash on off-white laid paper, lined

tea_voice_sources.text: Barberi defined as one of the most fertile architects of the Italian late 18th century, legacy preserved primarily through drawings rather than completed buildings

title: Elevation of a Building, Possibly a Kaffeehaus or Museum
medium: Pen and brown ink, brush and brown wash on off-white laid paper
credit: Museum purchase through gift of various donors and from Eleanor G. Hewitt Fund
caption_tea: This elevation, tentatively identified as a design for a coffeehouse or museum, belongs to the same body of inventive, largely unbuilt architectural fantasy that defines Giuseppe Barberi's surviving output — drawings, capricci, and theatrical set designs far outnumber anything he ever saw constructed.
caption_basic: Elevation of a Building, Possibly a Kaffeehaus or Museum by Giuseppe Barberi (ca. 1788–1789) -- Pen and brown ink, brush and brown wash on off-white laid paper

tea_voice_sources.text: Barberi's architectural legacy is primarily preserved through drawings rather than completed buildings, a prolific draftsman of ideal projects and capricci

title: Golden Pheasants in Spring
tags: Birds in art of China, Giuseppe Castiglione, Prunus in art, Bird-and-flower paintings in the National Palace Museum, Paintings of the Qing Dynasty in the National Palace Museum
caption_tea: Giuseppe Castiglione arrived in China as an Italian Jesuit missionary in 1714 and ended up spending 51 years as a court painter to three different Qing emperors, adopting the name Lang Shining. His real innovation was blending Western techniques — shading, realistic form — with Chinese brushwork conventions, creating a hybrid style the imperial court genuinely loved.
caption_basic: Golden Pheasants in Spring by Giuseppe Castiglione (18th century)

tea_voice_sources.text: Giuseppe Castiglione, an Italian Jesuit missionary who arrived in China in 1714, served as a court painter to the Kangxi, Yongzheng, and Qianlong emperors for 51 years under the Chinese name Lang Shining, blending Western realist technique with Chinese painting conventions.

title: Portrait of a Man, Possibly a Self-Portrait
artist: Velázquez (Diego Rodríguez de Silva y Velázquez)
caption_tea: The title's "possibly a self-portrait" comes from comparing the sitter's features to Velázquez's own face in Las Meninas, painted nearly two decades later -- the same heavy-lidded eyes and thick mustache, aged by time but unmistakably similar.
caption_basic: Portrait of a Man, Possibly a Self-Portrait by Velázquez (Diego Rodríguez de Silva y Velázquez) (ca. 1635) -- Oil on canvas
twist_hook: Demoted in 1979. Reinstated in 2009 -- from under the grime.
twist_story: Jules Bache paid dealer Joseph Duveen $1.125 million for this as a genuine Velázquez in 1926, and bequeathed it to the Met in 1949. By 1979, decades of yellowed varnish had dulled its color and blurred its brushwork past confident attribution, and the Museum downgraded it to "workshop of Velázquez." In 2009, conservator Michael Gallagher's cleaning changed that: murky greenish tones resolved into gray, and fine, confident brushwork emerged that scholars recognized as the master's own hand. Art historian Jonathan Brown put it simply: "The picture has been under my nose all my life." It re-entered the collection as an authentic Velázquez, not a copy.

title: Portfolio II, Plate 59: Judith-Mohave
credit: Presented by Mrs. James H. Hoyt, Elton Hoyt, II, and Mrs. Amasa Stone Mather in memory of James H. Hoyt
caption_tea: Edward Curtis spent four decades and more than 40,000 photographs trying to document Native American life before it "vanished" — a mission rooted in the era's belief that Indigenous cultures were doomed to disappear. To make that vision work, he paid sitters to pose, supplied his own costumes, and staged scenes that often had little to do with how his subjects actually lived in 1903. This photogravure is part of that vast, beautiful, and deeply contested project.
caption_basic: Portfolio II, Plate 59: Judith-Mohave by Edward S. Curtis (1903) -- photogravure

tea_voice_sources.text: Curtis's The North American Indian project (1907–1930) involved paid poses, supplied costumes, and staged compositions rooted in the 'vanishing race' ideology of ethnographic salvage photography popular at the time — a practice now widely critiqued by historians and Indigenous scholars.
